Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)

| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-67644", "CVE-2026-28277", "CVE-2026-27022")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

status: experimental

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("03bbc4fa1fd784276da135ab62fef85aaddea66e6eb176d7e59c3398f818b153") or SHA1 in~ ("03bbc4fa1fd784276da135ab62fef85aaddea66e6eb176d7e59c3398f818b153") or MD5 in~ ("03bbc4fa1fd784276da135ab62fef85aaddea66e6eb176d7e59c3398f818b153")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("03bbc4fa1fd784276da135ab62fef85aaddea66e6eb176d7e59c3398f818b153") or SHA1 in~ ("03bbc4fa1fd784276da135ab62fef85aaddea66e6eb176d7e59c3398f818b153") or MD5 in~ ("03bbc4fa1fd784276da135ab62fef85aaddea66e6eb176d7e59c3398f818b153")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["03bbc4fa1fd784276da135ab62fef85aaddea66e6eb176d7e59c3398f818b153"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

INTERPOL Operation Takes Down Sniper Dz Phishing Platform, Arrests Administrator

The Hacker News
2026-06-12 12 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

An INTERPOL-led operation last month resulted in the disruption of Sniper Dz, a decade-long phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) platform, Group-IB said Thursday. The effort, codenamed Operation Ramz, took place between October 2025 and February 2026, and saw authorities from 13 countries in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region making 201 arrests. Included among them was Guedz, the primary

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Raviral.com Sniper Dz kit endpoints accessed (k_fac.php / track.js) · [LLM] Phishing email click landing on Sniper Dz infrastructure (URL/click correlation) · [LLM] Brand-impersonating phishing pages on abused free-hosting platforms (Sniper Dz pattern) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Sniper Dz seized phishing infrastructure callback (post-takedown beacons) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Sniper Dz seized phishing infrastructure callback (post-takedown beacons) AICommand & Control High
Hunts internal hosts resolving or connecting to Sniper Dz / Joker Dz infrastructure domains seized during INTERPOL Operation Ramz. Any post-takedown beacon to these domains indicates a pre-existing compromise: dormant malware, browser-stored phishing-page bookmarks being clicked, or a victim whose stolen credentials are still being replayed from a host that's reaching the staging infra. Rationale: All 13 domains are taken verbatim from the article's pre-extracted IOC bundle for Sniper Dz / Joker Dz infrastructure seized by INTERPOL. Any callback to seized infrastructure is high-fidelity because the platform was taken offline in Feb 2026 — legitimate traffic should be zero. Cross-reference with the Group-IB / Unit 42 (Oct 2024) Sniper Dz writeups referenced in the article.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security-research sandbox detonation (any.run, Hybrid Analysis worker subnets) resolving seized domains as part of historical sample replay
  • Threat-intel enrichment platforms (Recorded Future, Anomali) doing periodic IOC validation from corporate egress
  • Vulnerability scanners with web-crawl modes hitting the IOC list
  • Researchers / red-teamers replaying old phishing PCAPs in a lab subnet that egresses through corporate proxy
  • Web filters that prefetch / categorize URLs from blocklists they pull themselves
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MpCmdRun.exe","smartscreen.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files\\Windows Defender" and DeviceName !startswith "sandbox-" and DeviceName !startswith "sb-"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the initiating process and parent for the connection on the implicated host. Determine whether it's a browser (user clicked an old bookmark / opened an archived email), a sandbox VM, or an unknown process (likely dormant stealer). Check the host's mail history for the URL. Step 2 (contain): Sinkhole all 13 domains at the proxy / DNS resolver immediately; this should be a permanent blocklist. Isolate the host if the calling process is non-browser. Force a password reset for the implicated user across SSO and externally-facing brand accounts (PayPal, Facebook, Steam, Netflix) given the credential-theft objective of the platform. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot the host's AAD sign-in history for the past 90 days against impossible-travel / new-MFA-device events. Sweep the org for any other host that resolved any seized domain in the last 180 days using the same IOC list.

Raviral.com Sniper Dz kit endpoints accessed (k_fac.php / track.js) AIDelivery High
Hunts HTTP/S access to two highly-specific Sniper Dz kit URLs documented by Group-IB: `/k_fac.php` (the Facebook-template credential submission endpoint) and `/host_style/style/js-track/track.js` (the per-victim tracking script). Either path appearing on the wire from an internal host is a strong indicator that a user is sitting on a live Sniper Dz phishing page on the seized infrastructure or a mirror. Rationale: `/k_fac.php` and `/host_style/style/js-track/track.js` are kit-specific filenames pulled from the article's IOC bundle (Group-IB analysis of seized raviral.com hosting). These paths have no legitimate use outside the Sniper Dz Facebook phishing template, so a single hit is high-confidence. Combining path-match with host=raviral.com catches mirrored/cloned kits even if the domain changes.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1056.003
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A blue-team detonation lab fetching the IOC URL for signature development
  • Researcher pulling the kit source via curl/wget from a workstation behind the corporate proxy
  • An automated phishing-takedown vendor (PhishLabs, Netcraft) scanning from the corporate IP space
  • Mirror-by-coincidence: an unrelated CMS that happens to expose /k_fac.php — verify the Referer / Host pairing
  • Search-engine crawler image rendering of archived screenshots that embed track.js
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("-IOC","--ioc","threat-intel","sandbox")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): For the matching host, pull the full browser session — Referer chain, parent process of the browser tab, and the exact URL preceding the kit-path fetch. If the parent is Outlook/Teams/explorer.exe via a link-click, treat as a confirmed live phishing visit. Step 2 (contain): Block raviral.com plus the two kit paths at the egress proxy. Reset the user's credentials for any brand the kit template impersonated (the article lists PayPal, Facebook, Instagram, Yahoo, Netflix, Steam as primary targets — Facebook is the `_fac` template). Revoke active AAD sessions and require MFA re-enrollment. Step 3 (hunt): Search the prior 48h of EmailEvents for any URL pointing at raviral.com or the other 12 seized domains for this recipient, and pivot across all internal users who received the same NetworkMessageId thread.

Phishing email click landing on Sniper Dz infrastructure (URL/click correlation) AIDelivery High
Correlates Defender for O365 Safe-Links click telemetry against the 13 seized Sniper Dz / Joker Dz domains. A `ClickAllowed` or `ClickedThrough` to any of these URLs proves the user reached a credential-harvesting page — a higher-fidelity signal than passive email delivery alone. Rationale: Joins inbound delivered email containing any of the 13 article-listed Sniper Dz domains to a Safe-Links click event proving the user actually reached the credential-capture page. The IOC list is verbatim from the article's pre-extracted bundle. Falcon LogScale left empty: FDR does not ship M365 Defender email/URL-click telemetry.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security awareness training platforms (KnowBe4, Cofense PhishMe) using these domains as decoys in simulated phishing — filter by known campaign sender
  • Threat-intel analysts forwarding phishing samples to a shared mailbox, then clicking from a triage console
  • User submits a phishing report through the Outlook 'Report Phish' button which clicks the URL in a sandboxed renderer
  • Mail with the URL gets archived to a researcher's quarantine inbox and the link is opened from there
  • Press-release / news article that legitimately links to a sniperdz.com forensic summary
Suppression filter
| where AccountUpn !in~ ("phishreport@contoso.com","abuse@contoso.com","soc@contoso.com") and IPAddress !in ("<known SOC sandbox egress IP>","<KnowBe4 simulator egress>")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the NetworkMessageId from the click and inspect EmailEvents for sender authentication (SPF/DKIM/DMARC), DeliveryLocation, and whether other recipients in the same thread also clicked. Look up the user's role in IdentityInfo to assess credential-blast-radius. Step 2 (contain): Force a password reset and revoke active sessions for the clicking user via Azure AD. Soft-delete the message from all recipients with Threat Explorer / `Soft-Delete`. Add the matched URL+domain to the tenant block list. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot AADSignInEventsBeta for the clicking user looking for sign-ins within 2-6h of the click from unusual countries / new IPs / non-compliant devices. Sweep EmailEvents for any other inbound mail with URLs to the 12 sibling domains within the last 30d.

Brand-impersonating phishing pages on abused free-hosting platforms (Sniper Dz pattern) AIDelivery Medium
Hunting query for the structural signature of Sniper Dz phishing pages: brand keywords (PayPal, Facebook, Instagram, Netflix, Steam, Yahoo, Free Fire / Garena, PUBG — the named targets in the article) embedded in the subdomain or path of free-hosting platforms (github.io, netlify.app, glitch.me, pantheonsite.io, 000webhostapp.com, epizy.com, blogspot.*). Surfaces unseen Sniper Dz / Joker Dz mirrors that re-spawn after the seizure, plus copycat PhaaS using the same hosting playbook. Rationale: Pattern extracted from the 13 article-listed Sniper Dz IOCs: 8 of them are brand- or lure-keyword subdomains on free hosting (github.io, netlify.app, glitch.me, pantheonsite.io, 000webhostapp.com, epizy.com, blogspot.be). Article says the platform deployed 80 templates across 30 brands in 5 languages and 20,000+ domains have been associated — first-seen hunting against this signature catches mirrors and copycat PhaaS operators using the same playbook.
ATT&CKT1583.001 T1566.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate brand-run microsites on Netlify/Vercel (some companies host promo pages this way) — verify by checking SSL cert SAN list
  • Researchers/students publishing fan sites or CTF write-ups containing brand names
  • Open-source projects hosted on GitHub Pages with names that coincidentally include 'login' or 'secure'
  • Legitimate gaming-community sites for Free Fire / PUBG / Garena hosted on free platforms — common in MENA / SEA
  • Brand-protection vendors crawling these patterns from corporate egress
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !startswith "https://docs." and RemoteUrl !startswith "https://help." and RemoteUrl !contains "/issues/" and RemoteUrl !contains "/blob/" and RemoteUrl !contains "/pull/"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): For each first-seen hit, render the URL in a sandbox and verify it's a credential-capture page; check the page source for `track.js`, `k_fac.php`, or form posts to raviral.com / sniperdz.com infrastructure (same template family). Pull WHOIS / GitHub repo owner if applicable. Step 2 (contain): Block the domain at the proxy. If users from your org reached the page, force credential reset for the impersonated brand's corporate SSO (if applicable) and revoke active sessions. Report to the hosting provider's abuse endpoint (GitHub, Netlify, Glitch all have rapid takedown). Step 3 (hunt): Extend the baseline window to 180d to surface long-tail Sniper Dz mirrors. Pivot the malicious URL into EmailEvents/EmailUrlInfo to find the delivery vector and the full recipient list.
let BrandKeywords = dynamic(["paypal","facebook","fbpage","instagram","netflix","steam","yahoo","freefire","free-fire","garena","pubg","whatsapp","tiktok","signin","login","secure","verify","reward","giveaway","prize","redeem","voting","v0ting"]);

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ivanti Sentry CVE-2026-10520 handleMessage exploit attempt (commandexec XML) AIExploitation High
Detects HTTP POST requests to the unauthenticated /mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage endpoint on Ivanti Sentry — the exact endpoint the public watchTowr PoC targets for CVE-2026-10520 root RCE. The payload embeds an XML <commandexec><reqandres> block parsed as an internal configuration command. Rationale: Endpoint /mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage is the exact vulnerable controller (ConfigServiceController) named in the watchTowr labs write-up and Horizon3 advisory; the POST method + unauthenticated path is a near-zero-FP signature for the public PoC. Falcon LogScale left blank because FDR does not ship Sentry Tomcat access logs by default. Defender DeviceNetworkEvents query catches admin-workstation-side egress to the URL but the WAF/proxy is the authoritative source. Cross-checked against: • https://labs.watchtowr.com/more-evidence-that-words-dont-mean-what-we-thought-they-meant-ivanti-sentry-pre-auth-os-command-injection-cve-2026-10520/ • https://horizon3.ai/attack-research/vulnerabilities/cve-2026-10520/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/10/ivanti-sentry-cve-2026-10520-cve-2026-10523/ • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-10520-cve-2026-10523-multiple-critical-vulnerabilities-affecting-ivanti-sentry/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004

  • Internal patch validation scripts replaying the PoC URI from a security-team jump host
  • WAF or load-balancer health-probes that include the path in monitoring
  • Ivanti TAC support pulling diagnostics through the management interface

| where not (SourceIP in ("<tenable_scanner_ip>", "<qualys_scanner_ip>")) and not (RequestClientApplication has_any ("Nessus", "Qualys", "Rapid7", "Tenable"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull the full WAF/proxy request — confirm POST body contains 'commandexec', 'reqandres', or 'execute system'. Check source IP against known scanner allowlists and threat-intel. Confirm the target Sentry build is below R10.5.2 / R10.6.2 / R10.7.1. 2) Contain: If source IP is external/unknown, block at perimeter and ACL the Sentry admin interface to management network only. If exploitation confirmed, isolate the Sentry appliance and failover to a peer. 3) Hunt: Pivot to UC2 (shell from Tomcat/Java on the appliance) within ±10 min of the request. Inventory all Sentry instances via UC3 and inspect for unauthorized admin accounts, modified web roots, and unexpected outbound connections (UC4).

Shell or recon binary spawned by Tomcat/Java on Ivanti Sentry (CVE-2026-10520 post-exploitation) AIExploitation High
Detects a shell (sh/bash/dash) or recon/download tool (curl/wget/nc/python/perl) spawned by the Tomcat/Java service that hosts the Ivanti Sentry web app. Because CVE-2026-10520 yields root RCE through the ConfigServiceController handler, successful exploitation manifests as a non-Java child of the Sentry Tomcat process — an event with no legitimate baseline on a production appliance. Rationale: Ivanti Sentry's web app runs under Tomcat/Java; the ConfigServiceController flaw lets an unauth caller pipe arbitrary commands to system(), so a non-Java child of the Sentry Tomcat process is the cleanest possible compromise signal. watchTowr and Horizon3 PoCs both demonstrate `id` and `whoami` as initial recon, so those names are included. Process names sourced from the same lab write-ups corroborated against Ivanti Sentry's Linux runtime; requires MDE Linux / Falcon / auditd shipped from the appliance. Cross-checked against: • https://horizon3.ai/attack-research/vulnerabilities/cve-2026-10520/ • https://labs.watchtowr.com/more-evidence-that-words-dont-mean-what-we-thought-they-meant-ivanti-sentry-pre-auth-os-command-injection-cve-2026-10520/ • https://socradar.io/blog/ivanti-sentrys-cve-2026-10520-rce/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Ivanti-supplied maintenance or upgrade scripts (R10.x release installers spawn sh from Java for cert rotation and DB schema upgrades)
  • Authorized administrator running 'mics' CLI utilities that the Tomcat user invokes through Runtime.exec()
  • Monitoring agents (Datadog/Splunk UF) executing shell-based health probes scoped to the Tomcat user
  • Cron-scheduled log-rotation or backup jobs running under the Tomcat service account
  • Vendor support pulling diagnostics via the management console which legitimately spawns 'id', 'uname'
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("mics_diagnostic","mics_upgrade","/opt/mobileiron/scripts/health","logrotate")) and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "-Djava.security.policy" and ProcessCommandLine has "backup")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Reconstruct the full Tomcat child-process tree on the appliance — look for stacked shells, network tools, or downloaders. Capture the corresponding /mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage HTTP request within ±30 sec from WAF/proxy logs (UC1). Confirm appliance build is below R10.5.2 / R10.6.2 / R10.7.1. 2) Contain: Network-isolate the Sentry appliance immediately; snapshot disk + memory. Failover mobile-device traffic to a redundant Sentry. Rotate any creds the appliance stores (LDAP bind, cert keys, K8s/EMM API tokens). 3) Hunt: Look for new local accounts, modified /home/* or web-root files, unexpected SSH key additions, cron entries, and outbound connections (UC4). Pivot to all other Sentry hosts in inventory (UC3) and assume any unpatched + internet-exposed instance is compromised per Shadowserver guidance.

   or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"/opt/mobileiron/", @"/opt/ivanti/", @"/var/lib/tomcat", @"/usr/share/tomcat", @"/mi/")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ksh","nc","ncat","curl","wget","python","python3","perl","ruby","id","whoami","uname","hostname")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"

Ivanti Sentry instances vulnerable to CVE-2026-10520 / CVE-2026-10523 AIReconnaissance High
Inventory pivot identifying Ivanti Sentry appliances still running pre-R10.5.2 / R10.6.2 / R10.7.1 builds and therefore vulnerable to CVE-2026-10520 and CVE-2026-10523. Drives BOD 26-04 3-day patching remediation and feeds the exposure / hunt UCs. Rationale: CVE IDs are taken verbatim from the BleepingComputer article (CVE-2026-10520) and the Rapid7 / Help Net Security advisories that disclosed the companion CVE-2026-10523. Fixed versions R10.5.2 / R10.6.2 / R10.7.1 are from the Ivanti advisory cited by Horizon3. Joining DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing prioritises the assets that satisfy BOD 26-04's 'publicly exposed online' patching trigger. Sigma / Datadog / Falcon / CloudWatch left empty — this is a vulnerability-inventory pivot, not a single-event detection. Cross-checked against: • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/10/ivanti-sentry-cve-2026-10520-cve-2026-10523/ • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-10520-cve-2026-10523-multiple-critical-vulnerabilities-affecting-ivanti-sentry/ • https://horizon3.ai/attack-research/vulnerabilities/cve-2026-10520/

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Decommissioned Sentry appliance still listed in inventory but powered off
  • Mismatched product fingerprint where the scanner tagged Ivanti EPMM as Sentry (related Ivanti products share signatures)
  • Test/lab Sentry instance intentionally kept on old build for regression testing in an isolated VLAN
  • Sentry deployed in HA pair where the secondary inherits the vuln tag from a queued sync
Response runbook
1) Triage: Filter to IsInternetFacing == true first — those are the 3-day BOD 26-04 priority. Confirm running build and patch path (R10.5.2 / R10.6.2 / R10.7.1 depending on branch). Cross-check against ITAM for decommissioned/lab hosts. 2) Contain: For each internet-facing vuln instance, immediately restrict /mics/ admin paths to management network at the edge (firewall ACL or WAF rule) until patched. Schedule emergency change within the 3-day window. 3) Hunt: For any host that has been internet-exposed and unpatched for >24 hours since 2026-06-10, assume compromise per Shadowserver guidance — run UC1 (exploit attempt) and UC2 (post-ex shell) against the last 30 days of telemetry for those hosts.

External / non-internal HTTP access to Ivanti Sentry /mics admin portal AIDelivery Medium
Surfaces internet-sourced HTTP requests to the Ivanti Sentry administrative /mics path tree, which is the exposed attack surface CVE-2026-10520 abuses. Shadowserver counted ~50 Sentry admin portals visible from the internet and warned that unpatched ones are likely already compromised, so any external touch of /mics is treated as a hunt-worthy pre-cursor event. Rationale: /mics is the management URI namespace for Ivanti Sentry / MobileIron Sentry — Horizon3 and watchTowr both root the vulnerable controller under it, and the Shadowserver visibility into 'Sentry admin portals exposed online' relies on the same path being reachable. Combining external source IP + admin path tree gives a reasonable hunt for both opportunistic scanning and targeted exploitation. Falcon LogScale empty because FDR doesn't ship Sentry HTTP access logs; CloudWatch empty because Sentry is on-prem. Cross-checked against: • https://hellorecon.com/blog/cve-2026-10520 • https://www.darkreading.com/vulnerabilities-threats/max-severity-ivanti-sentry-flaw-exploited-24-hours • https://gbhackers.com/ivanti-command-injection-flaw/
ATT&CKT1190 T1133 T1595.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Administrators accessing the Sentry admin portal from a corporate egress IP that isn't recognised as internal RFC1918 (e.g. NAT'd cloud bastion)
  • Approved Shodan/Censys/BinaryEdge crawler hits — high volume, low intent
  • MobileIron-enrolled devices on cellular networks checking in (typically /asfV3 or /mifs/c not /mics — investigate if /mics)
  • Vendor-side health checks from Ivanti's own scanning infrastructure
  • Third-party SOC monitoring services scanning the exposure on a schedule
Suppression filter
| where not (SourceIP in ("<shodan_cidr>","<censys_cidr>","<binaryedge_cidr>")) and not (RequestClientApplication has_any ("Shodan","Censys","BinaryEdge","InternetCensus"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: Bucket source IPs by ASN — separate research scanners (Shodan/Censys/BinaryEdge) from threat actors. For non-scanner IPs, dig the full request stream for the UC1 handleMessage exploit URI. 2) Contain: ACL the Sentry admin interface to management-network-only at the perimeter. If the Sentry version is below R10.5.2 / R10.6.2 / R10.7.1 and has been externally reachable for >24h, treat as presumed-compromised and follow UC2 containment runbook. 3) Hunt: Correlate the source IPs against UC1 hits in the same timeframe. Search threat-intel feeds (ThreatFox, AlienVault OTX) for these IPs against the CVE-2026-10520 campaign. Run UC3 to confirm patch status of every Sentry instance the org operates.

title: External HTTP Access to Ivanti Sentry Admin Portal
id: 5c6d7e8f-9a0b-4c3d-be4f-5a6b7c8d9e0f
description: Detects HTTP requests to Ivanti Sentry / MobileIron Sentry administrative endpoints (/mics/, /mifs/, /deviceadmin) sourced from outside RFC1918 space. Shadowserver tracked ~50 such admin portals exposed during CVE-2026-10520 in-the-wild exploitation.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-gives-feds-3-days-to-patch-ivanti-flaw-exploited-in-attacks/
  - https://hellorecon.com/blog/cve-2026-10520
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/12

  category: webserver
detection:
  selection_path:

      - '/mics/'
      - '/mifs/'

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Over 73,000 French govt employees affected in Tchap messenger breach

BleepingComputer
2026-06-12 7 use cases 1 technique 5 kill-chain phases detected

The French government revealed that a recent breach of its Tchap encrypted messaging platform affects the accounts of over 73,000 employees in the French public sector. [...]

ATT&CKT1059.001
Domainstchap.gouv.fr matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Bulk user-profile enumeration via Tchap Matrix /publicRooms API
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Anomalous endpoint authentication to Tchap (tchap.gouv.fr) — possible hijacked account
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] PowerShell with hardcoded LDAP bind credentials (Tchap-style leak) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Bulk Matrix/Tchap public room scraping (high-volume API fetches per single account) · [LLM] Large outbound transfer from endpoint to Tchap/Matrix FQDNs (potential 13.5GB-style exfil)
Anomalous endpoint authentication to Tchap (tchap.gouv.fr) — possible hijacked account AIDelivery Low
Hunts for first-time-seen or unusual endpoints initiating sessions to the Tchap web/Matrix endpoints (tchap.gouv.fr, matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr). The DINUM breach was initiated by an attacker authenticating to Tchap from a compromised account after social engineering, so a French public-sector tenant should watch for new device/IP pairings hitting those FQDNs. Rationale: The article names the Tchap platform domain explicitly (tchap.gouv.fr) and the Matrix federation FQDN visible in the leaked sample (matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr). First-seen-by-org joins against a 60-day baseline are the cleanest way to surface a hijacked account hitting Tchap from an endpoint that's never authenticated there before. Cross-checked against: • https://www.numerique.gouv.fr/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078/
ATT&CKT1078 T1566
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • New French govt staff onboarded to Tchap from a new device
  • BYOD laptop joining the network and resolving Tchap for the first time
  • Mobile-roaming users whose device ID changes after reimage
  • Pen-testing tooling probing the Tchap web origin from a non-standard host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe","safari.exe") or InitiatingProcessAccountUpn !endswith "@gouv.fr"
Response runbook
Triage: confirm whether the user/device pair is a genuine new Tchap onboarding via HR/IT records and whether the source IP geo matches expected work location. Contain: if unrecognised, force Tchap session revocation through DINUM and rotate Entra ID/AD password + MFA tokens for the user. Hunt: pivot on the same DeviceId for traffic to other gouv.fr SaaS (cloud.gouv.fr, ANSSI portals) and for outbound posting of large file uploads in the 24 h after first sighting.
let Baseline = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(60d) .. ago(7d))
    | where RemoteUrl has_any ("tchap.gouv.fr","matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr")
    | summarize by DeviceId, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("tchap.gouv.fr","matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr")
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on DeviceId, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Conns=count(), Urls=make_set(RemoteUrl, 25)
          by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP
| order by FirstSeen desc
let Baseline = ImDnsActivity
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(60d) .. ago(7d))
    | where DnsQuery has_any ("tchap.gouv.fr","matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr")
    | summarize by SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername;
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("tchap.gouv.fr","matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr")
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Queries=count(), Names=make_set(DnsQuery, 25) by SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, SrcHostname
| order by FirstSeen desc

Bulk Matrix/Tchap public room scraping (high-volume API fetches per single account) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for a single account or endpoint making an abnormally high count of HTTPS requests to the Tchap Matrix endpoints in a short window — modelling the attacker's claim of scraping ~650,000 messages and 73k profiles via the public-room APIs (/_matrix/client/r0/rooms/.../messages, /sync, /publicRooms). Rationale: The article cites exact scraping volumes (650,000 messages, 73,467 profiles, 13.5 GB media) — the attacker had to drive the Matrix HTTP API at a rate far above interactive use. Bucketed request-count thresholds against the named Tchap/Matrix FQDNs catch the rate, not the destination (which is legitimate). Cross-checked against: • https://spec.matrix.org/v1.10/client-server-api/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1213/
ATT&CKT1005 T1530 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Tchap Element/Web client doing initial /sync after offline period (catch-up)
  • Tchap admin / e-discovery search across many public rooms
  • Backup or compliance archival agents pulling room history
  • Synapse-to-Synapse federation traffic on a self-hosted relay (only if customer runs one)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("element.exe","element-desktop.exe","tchap.exe")
Response runbook
Triage: look at the user's last 30 days of Tchap usage volume and compare. Contain: if outlier, push immediate Tchap session revoke via DINUM, force AD password reset, isolate host with Defender Live Response. Hunt: pivot to whether the same host then uploaded files to external storage (Mega, Google Drive, Telegram, ThreatMon-linked C2) within 24 h.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("tchap.gouv.fr","matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr")
| summarize Connections=count(), DistinctRemoteIPs=dcount(RemoteIP), Bucket=bin(Timestamp, 10m)
          by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, InitiatingProcessFileName
| where Connections > 500    // empirically a Tchap desktop client averages <50 conns / 10 min
| order by Connections desc

          by SrcUsername, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname

| order by Requests desc

PowerShell with hardcoded LDAP bind credentials (Tchap-style leak) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts PowerShell processes / .ps1 files that contain hardcoded LDAP bind credentials (LDAP:// URI + System.DirectoryServices binding + plaintext password or NetworkCredential constructor). The threat actor exfiltrated exactly this artifact from Tchap repositories, so detecting these scripts at rest or at runtime catches both the leak source and downstream re-use of the leaked secrets. Rationale: Article: 'hardcoded LDAP credentials leaked via a PowerShell script.' Pairing the LDAP-bind tokens (LDAP://, DirectoryEntry, LdapConnection) with credential tokens (NetworkCredential, ConvertTo-SecureString, -Password) gives a token-aligned, high-fidelity match. Both conditions in one process command line is uncommon outside of the very leak pattern the attacker exposed. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/001/ • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.directoryservices
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1078 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin troubleshooting LDAP bind with a one-liner from a runbook
  • Vendor installer that binds to AD during setup (e.g. SCCM, Veeam)
  • Internal IAM lifecycle scripts that pass a service-account password
  • Red team / pentest using PowerView's Get-DomainUser -Credential
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has_any (@"\Program Files\Veeam\", @"\Program Files\Microsoft Configuration Manager\", @"\Program Files\WindowsPowerShell\Modules\ActiveDirectory\")
Response runbook
Triage: extract the credential string from CommandLine, look up the bind DN, and confirm whether the account is a real service account vs sample/test value. Contain: if the credential is real and bound to a privileged account, rotate the password immediately, revoke Kerberos tickets, and disable the script's source path. Hunt: search Defender DeviceFileEvents for the same .ps1 SHA256 in repos/file shares, and Sentinel SigninLogs / IdentityLogonEvents for binds using the exposed account from unexpected source IPs in the prior 90 days.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","powershell_ise.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","powershell_ise.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("LDAP://","DirectoryEntry","System.DirectoryServices.Protocols","System.DirectoryServices","LdapConnection","PrincipalContext")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("NetworkCredential","ConvertTo-SecureString","-Password","PasswordCredential","userPassword","bindDN","secret")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\pwsh.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\powershell_ise.exe"
     or ParentProcessName endswith @"\powershell.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith @"\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("LDAP://","DirectoryEntry","System.DirectoryServices.Protocols","System.DirectoryServices","LdapConnection","PrincipalContext")
| where CommandLine has_any ("NetworkCredential","ConvertTo-SecureString","-Password","PasswordCredential","userPassword","bindDN","secret")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: PowerShell with hardcoded LDAP bind credentials
id: 4d1b6a23-0a9f-4d1c-9a51-3e2c5a5c7e2d
status: experimental
description: Detects PowerShell invocations that combine an LDAP bind (LDAP:// URI or System.DirectoryServices/LdapConnection) with what looks like a hardcoded credential (NetworkCredential, ConvertTo-SecureString, -Password, userPassword), modelling the leaked-credential artifact from the 2026 Tchap DINUM breach.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/french-govt-says-tchap-breach-affected-over-73-000-accounts/
author: detection-engineering
date: 2026/06/12
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1552.001
  - attack.t1078
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_image:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\powershell_ise.exe'
  selection_ldap:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'LDAP://'
      - 'DirectoryEntry'
      - 'System.DirectoryServices'
      - 'LdapConnection'
      - 'PrincipalContext'
  selection_cred:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'NetworkCredential'
      - 'ConvertTo-SecureString'
      - '-Password'
      - 'PasswordCredential'
      - 'userPassword'
      - 'bindDN'
  condition: selection_image and selection_ldap and selection_cred
falsepositives:
  - Sysadmins running ad-hoc AD diagnostic scripts
  - Vendor installers that bind to AD during setup
level: medium

source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security) (@Image:(*\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\pwsh.EXE) OR @ParentImage:(*\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe)) (@CommandLine:*LDAP\:\/\/* OR @CommandLine:*DirectoryEntry* OR @CommandLine:*System.DirectoryServices* OR @CommandLine:*LdapConnection* OR @CommandLine:*PrincipalContext*) (@CommandLine:*NetworkCredential* OR @CommandLine:*ConvertTo-SecureString* OR @CommandLine:*\-Password* OR @CommandLine:*userPassword* OR @CommandLine:*bindDN*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh|powershell_ise)\.exe$/i
| regex("(?i)(LDAP:\/\/|DirectoryEntry|System\.DirectoryServices|LdapConnection|PrincipalContext)", field=CommandLine)
| regex("(?i)(NetworkCredential|ConvertTo-SecureString|-Password|PasswordCredential|userPassword|bindDN|secret)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
| sort(_count, order=desc)
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","powershell_ise.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process, "(?i)(LDAP://|DirectoryEntry|System\.DirectoryServices|LdapConnection|PrincipalContext)") AND match(process, "(?i)(NetworkCredential|ConvertTo-SecureString|password|userPassword|-pwd|secret|bind)") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","powershell_ise.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process, "(?i)(LDAP://|DirectoryEntry|System\.DirectoryServices|LdapConnection|PrincipalContext)") AND match(process, "(?i)(NetworkCredential|ConvertTo-SecureString|password|userPassword|-pwd|secret|bind)") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Large outbound transfer from endpoint to Tchap/Matrix FQDNs (potential 13.5GB-style exfil) AIActions on Objectives Low
Tracks per-host download volume against tchap.gouv.fr / matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr over a short window. The attacker claims to have pulled 13.5 GB of attachments — a single endpoint pulling multi-GB from Tchap stands out against typical interactive use (avatars, attachments, small media). Rationale: Article quantifies stolen volume at 13.5 GB. Per-hour byte-sum against the named Tchap FQDNs at the proxy is the cleanest pivot — Defender DeviceNetworkEvents lacks byte counts, so the Defender slot is intentionally empty; Sentinel CommonSecurityLog from the egress proxy carries SentBytes/ReceivedBytes. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1048/003/
ATT&CKT1048.003 T1020
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Tchap admin/e-discovery export operation
  • Backup agent archiving Tchap chats
  • User catching up after weeks offline (large initial /sync of attachments)
  • Power user in a media-heavy public room (architecture diagrams, video PoCs)
Suppression filter
| where SourceUserName !in~ ("svc-tchap-archive","svc-ediscovery") and SourceIP !in ("<known-backup-host-ips>")
Response runbook
Triage: confirm whether the user role legitimately involves bulk Tchap data handling and whether matching outbound transfers from the same host to non-gouv.fr destinations followed within 24 h. Contain: if not legitimate, suspend the user's Tchap session (DINUM revoke), isolate host with Defender Live Response. Hunt: search the same SourceIP / host for outbound posting to file-share or anonymisation services (mega.nz, anonfiles, transfer.sh, Tor exit nodes) in the following 48 h.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationHostName has_any ("tchap.gouv.fr","matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr")
   or RequestURL has_any ("tchap.gouv.fr","matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr")
| summarize TotalBytesIn=sum(toint(ReceivedBytes)), TotalBytesOut=sum(toint(SentBytes)), Requests=count(), Bucket=bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
          by SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName
| where TotalBytesIn > 1073741824    // 1 GiB / hour, well above interactive Tchap usage
| order by TotalBytesIn desc
source:(windows.sysmon OR linux.auditd OR fortinet OR paloalto) (@DestinationHostname:(*tchap.gouv.fr OR *matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr) OR @network.destination.domain:(*tchap.gouv.fr OR *matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr))
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 
| join({#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(tchap\.gouv\.fr|matrix\.agent\.education\.tchap\.gouv\.fr)$/i | groupBy([aid, FirstIP4Record], function=count())}, field=[aid, RemoteAddressIP4], include=[DomainName])
| bucket(span=1h, field=@timestamp)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, _bucket, DomainName], function=count(as=Conns))
| Conns > 5000
| sort(Conns, order=desc)
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true sum(Web.bytes_in) as bytes_in count from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*tchap.gouv.fr*" OR Web.url="*matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr*") by Web.src Web.user _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where bytes_in > 1073741824    // 1 GiB / hour from a single src is far above baseline | sort - bytes_in
| tstats summariesonly=false sum(Web.bytes_in) as bytes_in count from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*tchap.gouv.fr*" OR Web.url="*matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr*") by Web.src Web.user _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where bytes_in > 1073741824    // 1 GiB / hour from a single src is far above baseline | sort - bytes_in
Bulk user-profile enumeration via Tchap Matrix /publicRooms API AIReconnaissance Low
Hunts for endpoints driving the Matrix /publicRooms and /joined_members API endpoints to enumerate user identities (display name, email, avatar, organisation) at scale — the exact data set the attacker exfiltrated for 73,467 French civil servants. Rationale: Article: attacker collected 'last name, first name, email address, belonging entity and avatar' across 73,467 users. In Matrix that means hammering /publicRooms, /joined_members, and /profile/{userId}. Path-aware proxy detection threshold catches it; the 200-request / 30-distinct-URL bound is empirically above interactive use. Cross-checked against: • https://spec.matrix.org/v1.10/client-server-api/#listing-rooms • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1087/004/
ATT&CKT1087.004 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Tchap directory/admin doing legitimate user audit
  • New onboarded user clicking through many public rooms to find their team
  • Mobile sync after long offline period pulling member lists
  • Compliance tooling enumerating room membership for retention policy
Suppression filter
| where SrcUsername !in~ ("tchap-admin","svc-tchap-audit")
Response runbook
Triage: pull the user's Tchap role and recent HR activity; check whether the path mix (publicRooms vs joined_members) matches a known admin/audit workflow. Contain: if not legitimate, suspend the Tchap session, reset Entra/AD credentials, and notify CNIL counterparts at DINUM. Hunt: pivot to whether the same host then exported the enumerated data outbound (UC4) or pushed it to file-sharing/messaging platforms in the following 24 h.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("tchap.gouv.fr","matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("publicRooms","/joined_members","/members","profile")
| summarize EnumRequests=count(), DistinctUrls=dcount(RemoteUrl), Bucket=bin(Timestamp, 15m)
          by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, InitiatingProcessFileName
| where EnumRequests > 200 or DistinctUrls > 30
| order by EnumRequests desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any ("tchap.gouv.fr","matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr")
| where Url has_any ("publicRooms","/joined_members","/members","profile")
| summarize EnumRequests=count(), DistinctUrls=dcount(Url), Bucket=bin(TimeGenerated, 15m)
          by SrcUsername, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname
| where EnumRequests > 200 or DistinctUrls > 30
| order by EnumRequests desc
source:(windows.sysmon OR linux.auditd) (@DestinationHostname:(*tchap.gouv.fr OR *matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr) OR @network.destination.domain:(*tchap.gouv.fr OR *matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr)) (@http.url:*publicRooms* OR @http.url:*joined_members* OR @http.url:*/members* OR @http.url:*profile*)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(tchap\.gouv\.fr|matrix\.agent\.education\.tchap\.gouv\.fr)$/i
| bucket(span=15m, field=@timestamp)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, _bucket], function=count(as=Lookups))
| Lookups > 500
| sort(Lookups, order=desc)
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*tchap.gouv.fr*" OR Web.url="*matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr*") AND (Web.url="*publicRooms*" OR Web.url="*/joined_members*" OR Web.url="*/members*" OR Web.url="*profile*") by Web.src Web.user Web.url _time span=15m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | stats sum(count) as reqs dc(url) as distinctUrls by src user _time | where reqs > 200 OR distinctUrls > 30
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*tchap.gouv.fr*" OR Web.url="*matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr*") AND (Web.url="*publicRooms*" OR Web.url="*/joined_members*" OR Web.url="*/members*" OR Web.url="*profile*") by Web.src Web.user Web.url _time span=15m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | stats sum(count) as reqs dc(url) as distinctUrls by src user _time | where reqs > 200 OR distinctUrls > 30
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

logsource:
