Boot-to-WinRE command observed — shutdown /r /o or reagentc /boottore AIExploitation High
The GreatXML chain ends with 'Reboot to Windows Recovery Environment by holding Shift while clicking Restart'. Programmatic equivalents are shutdown.exe /r /o and reagentc.exe /boottore — both stage the next boot into WinRE. Catching either soon after a recovery-partition file write is the highest-fidelity 'exploit about to fire' signal. Rationale: Article describes the trigger step explicitly: 'Reboot to Windows Recovery Environment (WinRE) by holding Shift while clicking Restart in the Windows power menu.' shutdown.exe /r /o and reagentc.exe /boottore are the only command-line equivalents that achieve the same boot-to-WinRE state; flagging either after a recovery-partition write gives near-certain GreatXML detection.
ATT&CKT1542.005 T1529
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin remotely rebooting a laptop into WinRE for repair
  • Driver troubleshooting workflow needing Advanced Startup
  • Helpdesk-guided BitLocker recovery flow
  • Surface device firmware update prompting boot-to-WinRE
  • Enterprise reset/wipe via Intune company-portal initiating reagentc /boottore
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","Sense.exe","IntuneManagementExtension.exe","MicrosoftIntuneManagementExtension.exe")) | where not(ParentProcessName in~ ("explorer.exe") and ActorUsername in~ ("helpdesk","itsupport"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): If HasRecentDrop=true, treat as confirmed GreatXML — go straight to contain. Otherwise check the user, parent process, and whether a legitimate IT/repair ticket explains the WinRE boot. Step 2 (contain): If unauthorised, block the boot by suspending the host (Defender 'Isolate' + power-cycle from out-of-band management before the staged restart fires). Force rotation of the BitLocker recovery key for this device in Entra. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to all DeviceProcessEvents for the past 24h on this host — was MpCmdRun -WDOfflineScan run? Was an unattend.xml or ReAgent.xml dropped? If yes, treat the disk as compromised post-reboot.
let BootToWinRE = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where (FileName =~ "shutdown.exe" and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s/r\b" and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s/o\b")
         or (FileName =~ "reagentc.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/boottore")
    | where isnotempty(AccountName) and not(AccountName endswith "$")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName;
let RecoveryDrop = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where (FileName =~ "ReAgent.xml" and FolderPath has @"\Recovery\WindowsRE\")
         or (FileName =~ "unattend.xml" and FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)^[a-z]:\\unattend\.xml$")
    | project DropTime = Timestamp, DeviceName;
BootToWinRE
| join kind=leftouter RecoveryDrop on DeviceName
| extend HasRecentDrop = iif(DropTime between (Timestamp - 4h .. Timestamp), true, false)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, HasRecentDrop, DropTime
| order by HasRecentDrop desc, Timestamp desc
let BootToWinRE = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where (ActingProcessName =~ "shutdown.exe" and ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s/r\b" and ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s/o\b")
         or (ActingProcessName =~ "reagentc.exe" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "/boottore")
    | where isnotempty(ActorUsername) and not(ActorUsername endswith "$")
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName;
let RecoveryDrop = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where (TargetFileName =~ "ReAgent.xml" and TargetFilePath contains @"\Recovery\WindowsRE\")
         or (TargetFileName =~ "unattend.xml" and TargetFilePath matches regex @"(?i)^[a-z]:\\unattend\.xml$")
    | project DropTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname;
BootToWinRE
| join kind=leftouter RecoveryDrop on DvcHostname
| extend HasRecentDrop = iif(DropTime between (TimeGenerated - 4h .. TimeGenerated), true, false)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, HasRecentDrop, DropTime
| order by HasRecentDrop desc, TimeGenerated desc
title: Boot to Windows Recovery Environment Triggered
id: c4b27d61-5e9a-49a8-8b0e-72a4c6e3f1d0
description: Detects shutdown.exe /r /o or reagentc.exe /boottore — the programmatic equivalents of Shift+Restart used to enter WinRE for the GreatXML BitLocker bypass.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-greatxml-exploit-bypasses-windows.html
author: thn-usecases
date: 2026/06/12
tags:
  - attack.t1542.005
  - attack.t1529
  - attack.defense_evasion
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_shutdown:
    Image|endswith: '\shutdown.exe'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - ' /r'
      - ' /o'
  selection_reagentc:
    Image|endswith: '\reagentc.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: '/boottore'
  condition: selection_shutdown or selection_reagentc
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 ((@Image:(*\\shutdown.exe OR *\\Shutdown.exe) AND @CommandLine:(*" /r "* OR *" /r/o "*) AND @CommandLine:(*" /o "* OR *" /o/r "*)) OR (@Image:(*\\reagentc.exe OR *\\ReAgentc.exe OR *\\REAGENTC.EXE) AND @CommandLine:*"/boottore"*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ((ImageFileName=/\\shutdown\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/\s\/r\b/i AND CommandLine=/\s\/o\b/i) OR (ImageFileName=/\\reagentc\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/\/boottore/i))
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="shutdown.exe" AND Processes.process="*/o*" AND Processes.process="*/r*") OR (Processes.process_name="reagentc.exe" AND Processes.process="*/boottore*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where NOT match(user, "\\$$") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="shutdown.exe" AND Processes.process="*/o*" AND Processes.process="*/r*") OR (Processes.process_name="reagentc.exe" AND Processes.process="*/boottore*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where NOT match(user, "\\$$") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
reagentc.exe /setreimage or /setosimage — WinRE image repointing AIInstallation Medium
reagentc.exe is the only supported tool to register a new WinRE image (/setreimage) or OS image (/setosimage); both flags effectively let the caller pick which Recovery partition Windows boots when Shift+Restart fires. The GreatXML primitive depends on the recovery partition being read at boot — repointing it is a closely related abuse path that the same exploit family could leverage. Rationale: Article calls out the recovery partition as the staging surface; reagentc.exe is the canonical Windows-shipped binary for manipulating that partition's image registration. /setreimage and /setosimage with a user-writable path are the suspicious shapes; /enable can be used to flip WinRE back on after the malicious image is in place.
ATT&CKT1542.005 T1112
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin repairing WinRE after disk corruption with /setreimage \Recovery\WindowsRE
  • Windows feature update repointing WinRE during OS upgrade
  • reagentc /info called interactively for diagnostics
  • Endpoint management tool (Intune/SCCM) re-baselining WinRE state
  • Vendor OEM laptop refresh tooling restoring factory recovery image
Suppression filter
| where not(ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)/setreimage\s+[\"']?\\\\\?\\GLOBALROOT\\device\\harddisk\d+\\partition\d+\\Recovery\\WindowsRE[\"']?")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Check the target path supplied to /setreimage — legitimate use points at the OEM \Recovery\WindowsRE directory; attacker use points at a user-writable folder or new partition root. Step 2 (contain): If the image path is non-standard, isolate and revert WinRE config via reagentc /setreimage to the known-good path; rotate BitLocker recovery keys. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate with same-host MpCmdRun -WDOfflineScan and DeviceFileEvents writes to \Recovery\WindowsRE\ReAgent.xml within the previous 24h to confirm GreatXML staging.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "reagentc.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/setreimage", "/setosimage", "/enable", "/info")
| where isnotempty(AccountName) and not(AccountName endswith "$")
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("TrustedInstaller.exe","sysprep.exe","setup.exe","MoUsoCoreWorker.exe","WindowsUpdateBox.exe"))
| extend SuspiciousPath = iif(ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)/set(re|os)image\s+[\"']?[A-Z]:\\", true, false)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SuspiciousPath
| order by SuspiciousPath desc, Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName =~ "reagentc.exe"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/setreimage", "/setosimage", "/enable", "/info")
| where isnotempty(ActorUsername) and not(ActorUsername endswith "$")
| where not(ParentProcessName in~ ("TrustedInstaller.exe","sysprep.exe","setup.exe","MoUsoCoreWorker.exe","WindowsUpdateBox.exe"))
| extend SuspiciousPath = iif(ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)/set(re|os)image\s+[\"']?[A-Z]:\\", true, false)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, SuspiciousPath
| order by SuspiciousPath desc, TimeGenerated desc
title: reagentc.exe Used to Repoint Windows Recovery Environment
id: 1f7e54aa-9b32-4e0c-8e57-3b1a82f4d9a6
description: Detects use of reagentc.exe with /setreimage, /setosimage, or /enable — used to repoint or reactivate the WinRE image, a precursor to recovery-partition-based BitLocker bypass attacks such as GreatXML.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-greatxml-exploit-bypasses-windows.html
author: thn-usecases
date: 2026/06/12
tags:
  - attack.t1542.005
  - attack.defense_evasion
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\reagentc.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '/setreimage'
      - '/setosimage'
      - '/enable'
  filter_legit_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\TrustedInstaller.exe'
      - '\sysprep.exe'
      - '\setup.exe'
      - '\MoUsoCoreWorker.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter_legit_parent
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\reagentc.exe OR *\\ReAgentc.exe OR *\\REAGENTC.EXE) @CommandLine:(*/setreimage* OR */setosimage* OR */enable*) -@ParentImage:(*\\TrustedInstaller.exe OR *\\trustedinstaller.exe OR *\\sysprep.exe OR *\\setup.exe OR *\\MoUsoCoreWorker.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\reagentc\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/\/(setreimage|setosimage|enable)\b/i
| NOT (ParentBaseFileName=/(TrustedInstaller|sysprep|setup|MoUsoCoreWorker)\.exe$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="reagentc.exe" AND (Processes.process="*/setreimage*" OR Processes.process="*/setosimage*" OR Processes.process="*/enable*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where NOT match(parent_process_name, "(?i)(TrustedInstaller|setup|sysprep|MoUsoCoreWorker)\\.exe") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="reagentc.exe" AND (Processes.process="*/setreimage*" OR Processes.process="*/setosimage*" OR Processes.process="*/enable*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where NOT match(parent_process_name, "(?i)(TrustedInstaller|setup|sysprep|MoUsoCoreWorker)\\.exe") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
manage-bde.exe disable/unlock against system volume AIActions on Objectives High
GreatXML's stated objective is 'a shell spawned with unrestricted access to the BitLocker volume'. The follow-on attacker action — once the bypass shell is live OR during a YellowKey/GreatXML chain — is to use manage-bde.exe to suspend, disable, or unlock BitLocker so plaintext access persists across reboot. Detects the suspicious manage-bde verbs. Rationale: Article's described end-state: 'a shell spawned with unrestricted access to the BitLocker volume'. The deterministic follow-on for an attacker wanting persistent plaintext access is manage-bde -off / Disable-BitLocker. Both PowerShell cmdlet and manage-bde verbs are exact-string matches; -off in particular is rarely a routine admin action.
ATT&CKT1552.004 T1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Decommissioning workflow disabling BitLocker before disk wipe
  • Admin temporarily suspending BitLocker for firmware/BIOS update
  • Imaging team using manage-bde -unlock on a freshly-cloned volume
  • SCCM/Intune BitLocker policy remediation cycle
  • User running 'Turn off BitLocker' from Control Panel (which invokes manage-bde under the hood)
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("IntuneManagementExtension.exe","MicrosoftIntuneManagementExtension.exe","CcmExec.exe","MpCmdRun.exe")) | where not(ActingProcessCommandLine has "-status")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Check the parent process and user; legitimate decommissions come from IT admin accounts during change windows, not from explorer.exe in user sessions. Look back 24h for GreatXML precursors (MpCmdRun -WDOfflineScan, ReAgent.xml write, shutdown /r /o). Step 2 (contain): If unauthorised, isolate the device, force re-enable BitLocker via Intune, rotate the recovery key in Entra. If keys may have been read while disabled, treat the disk contents as compromised. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep org for any manage-bde -off / Disable-BitLocker in last 30 days that lacks a matching change ticket; sweep AAD audit logs for BitLocker recovery-key reads in the same window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (FileName =~ "manage-bde.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-off", "-protectors -disable", "-unlock", "-forcerecovery"))
   or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Disable-BitLocker", "Suspend-BitLocker"))
| where isnotempty(AccountName) and not(AccountName endswith "$")
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe","WindowsUpdateBox.exe","setup.exe"))
| extend TargetsSystemVolume = iif(ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s[a-z]:\s|\sC:\\\s*$|\s%SystemDrive%\s", true, false)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, TargetsSystemVolume
| order by TargetsSystemVolume desc, Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (ActingProcessName =~ "manage-bde.exe" and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("-off", "-protectors -disable", "-unlock", "-forcerecovery"))
   or (ActingProcessName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("Disable-BitLocker", "Suspend-BitLocker"))
| where isnotempty(ActorUsername) and not(ActorUsername endswith "$")
| where not(ParentProcessName in~ ("MsSense.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe","WindowsUpdateBox.exe","setup.exe"))
| extend TargetsSystemVolume = iif(ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s[a-z]:\s|\sC:\\\s*$|\s%SystemDrive%\s", true, false)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, TargetsSystemVolume
| order by TargetsSystemVolume desc, TimeGenerated desc
title: BitLocker Disabled or Unlocked via manage-bde or PowerShell
id: 2c8d419e-6f43-4a5b-b2e9-71f5c8a4d1b3
description: Detects use of manage-bde.exe with -off / -protectors -disable / -unlock / -forcerecovery, or PowerShell Disable-BitLocker / Suspend-BitLocker — the typical post-bypass step after a recovery-partition-based BitLocker attack like GreatXML or CVE-2026-45585 (YellowKey).
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-greatxml-exploit-bypasses-windows.html
author: thn-usecases
date: 2026/06/12
tags:

logsource:

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 ((@Image:(*\\manage-bde.exe OR *\\Manage-bde.exe OR *\\MANAGE-BDE.EXE) AND @CommandLine:(*" -off"* OR *"-protectors -disable"* OR *" -unlock"* OR *" -forcerecovery"*)) OR (@Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe) AND @CommandLine:(*Disable-BitLocker* OR *Suspend-BitLocker*)))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ((ImageFileName=/\\manage-bde\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/\s-(off|unlock|forcerecovery)\b/i) OR (ImageFileName=/\\manage-bde\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/-protectors\s+-disable/i) OR (ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/(Disable|Suspend)-BitLocker/i))
| NOT (ParentBaseFileName=/(TrustedInstaller|setup|WindowsUpdateBox|MsSense)\.exe$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="manage-bde.exe" AND (Processes.process="*-off*" OR Processes.process="*-protectors -disable*" OR Processes.process="*-unlock*" OR Processes.process="*-forcerecovery*")) OR (Processes.process_name="powershell.exe" AND (Processes.process="*Disable-BitLocker*" OR Processes.process="*Suspend-BitLocker*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where NOT match(user, "\\$$") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="manage-bde.exe" AND (Processes.process="*-off*" OR Processes.process="*-protectors -disable*" OR Processes.process="*-unlock*" OR Processes.process="*-forcerecovery*")) OR (Processes.process_name="powershell.exe" AND (Processes.process="*Disable-BitLocker*" OR Processes.process="*Suspend-BitLocker*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where NOT match(user, "\\$$") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-45585")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-45585")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-45585")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-45585")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Webserver process writes PHP-executable file to public web-root or upload directory (CVE-2026-48062) AIInstallation High
Detects php-fpm, nginx, httpd, w3wp, caddy or the php interpreter creating .php / .phar / .phtml / .phps / .pht files under common public web roots (public, webroot, htdocs, www, uploads, public_html). The CodeIgniter4 ext_in bypass advisory explicitly warns of this landing-on-disk artefact when applications save with the original client filename via $file->move($path). Rationale: Anchors on the article's explicit conditions: 'save uploads using original client filename', 'store uploads in a web-accessible directory', 'allow PHP files to run from that directory'. The webserver-account UID writing a PHP-executable extension under /public is precisely the post-validation-bypass artefact. Filename-extension list (.php/.phar/.phtml/.phps/.pht) covers all PHP-handler-mapped extensions and matches the article's exact bypass example (shell.php).
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003 T1036.008
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Composer install / git pull during a legitimate deploy, when the webserver UID writes vendored .php files into public/
  • CMS plugin or theme installer writing .php under public/uploads/ via an in-app admin upload (WordPress, Drupal extension store)
  • Dev environment with hot-reload writing into the document root under the webserver UID
  • CodeIgniter4 cache writers writing PHP cache shards to writable/cache (filter via the writable/ prefix)
  • Imagick or thumbnailer wrappers that legitimately move processed assets into /public/uploads/thumbs/ — if any are .php-suffixed (rare)
Suppression filter
and not (FolderPath has_any (@"\writable\","/writable/",@"\vendor\","/vendor/",@"\.git\","/.git/")) and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("composer","git pull","git checkout","git clone","deploy")) and not (FileName startswith "index.php")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the file at FolderPath\FileName from a forensic copy — confirm presence of webshell strings (eval, system, base64_decode, assert, passthru) or polyglot GIF/JFIF magic followed by `<?php`. Pull the SHA256 to VirusTotal / internal sandbox. Identify the upload endpoint by tracing InitiatingProcessId backwards through DeviceProcessEvents. 2) Contain: quarantine the file (rename to .quarantine, chmod 000), block the source IP at WAF, and disable the affected CodeIgniter4 application or stop the webserver if active exploitation is ongoing. 3) Hunt: pivot on InitiatingProcessId for outbound NetworkConnect/DnsRequest from php-fpm/w3wp in the next 24h, look for additional .php drops on neighbour hosts behind the same load balancer, and confirm CodeIgniter4 version inventory against CVE-2026-48062 (UC 4 below).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-fpm.exe","php-cgi.exe","httpd.exe","nginx.exe","w3wp.exe","caddy.exe","php.exe")
| where FileName endswith ".php" or FileName endswith ".phar" or FileName endswith ".phtml" or FileName endswith ".phps" or FileName endswith ".pht"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\public\", @"\webroot\", @"\htdocs\", @"\www\", @"\uploads\", @"\public_html\", "/public/", "/webroot/", "/htdocs/", "/www/", "/uploads/", "/public_html/")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, FileSize, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType =~ "FileCreated" or EventType =~ "FileRenamed" or EventType =~ "FileModified"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","php-cgi","httpd","nginx","w3wp","caddy","php.exe","php")
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("php","phar","phtml","phps","pht")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\public\",@"\webroot\",@"\htdocs\",@"\www\",@"\uploads\",@"\public_html\","/public/","/webroot/","/htdocs/","/www/","/uploads/","/public_html/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, TargetFileSize, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Webserver / PHP interpreter writes PHP-executable file to public web root (CVE-2026-48062)
id: 2c54e1a8-3b4e-4d8c-9a9a-3f7b2a1c4d6e
description: |
  Detects webserver / interpreter processes (php-fpm, php-cgi, nginx, httpd, w3wp, caddy, php) writing
  PHP-executable files (.php/.phar/.phtml/.phps/.pht) under common public web-roots. This is the
  landing-on-disk artefact of the CodeIgniter4 ext_in upload-validation bypass (CVE-2026-48062) where
  a file named shell.php with GIF-like content passed `ext_in[avatar,gif]`.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2gr4-ppc7-7mhx
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/12
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.t1505.003
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.t1036.008
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_process:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\php-fpm.exe'
      - '\php-cgi.exe'
      - '\httpd.exe'
      - '\nginx.exe'
      - '\w3wp.exe'
      - '\caddy.exe'
      - '\php.exe'
  selection_ext:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '.php'
      - '.phar'
      - '.phtml'
      - '.phps'
      - '.pht'
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\public\'
      - '\webroot\'
      - '\htdocs\'
      - '\www\'
      - '\uploads\'
      - '\public_html\'
  condition: selection_process and selection_ext and selection_path
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate composer install / git pull writing new PHP modules under public during deploy
  - CMS plugin or theme installer dropping PHP includes in public web-root
  - Developer hot-reload pushing PHP into the public dir on a non-prod host
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\\php-fpm.exe OR *\\PHP-FPM.exe OR *\\php-cgi.exe OR *\\httpd.exe OR *\\HTTPD.exe OR *\\nginx.exe OR *\\Nginx.exe OR *\\w3wp.exe OR *\\W3WP.exe OR *\\caddy.exe OR *\\php.exe OR *\\PHP.exe) @TargetFilename:(*.php OR *.phar OR *.phtml OR *.phps OR *.pht) (@TargetFilename:(*\\public\\* OR *\\webroot\\* OR *\\htdocs\\* OR *\\www\\* OR *\\uploads\\* OR *\\public_html\\*) OR @TargetFilename:(*/public/* OR */webroot/* OR */htdocs/* OR */www/* OR */uploads/* OR */public_html/*))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| ContextImageFileName=/(php-fpm|php-cgi|httpd|nginx|w3wp|caddy|php)\.exe$/i
| TargetFileName=/\.(php|phar|phtml|phps|pht)$/i
| regex("(\\\\|/)(public|webroot|htdocs|www|uploads|public_html)(\\\\|/)", field=TargetFileName, flags="i")
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count(as=writes))
ENDPOINT

Webserver / PHP interpreter spawns shell or LOLBin — post-upload RCE indicator AIExploitation High
Detects php-fpm, php-cgi, nginx, httpd, w3wp, caddy or php.exe directly spawning cmd/powershell/sh/bash or LOLBins (whoami, net, certutil, curl, wget, bitsadmin). The CodeIgniter4 ext_in bypass culminates in arbitrary code execution when the dropped PHP file is requested — this catches the resulting child process even when the on-disk artefact is missed. Rationale: Article's stated impact is 'arbitrary code execution' via the dropped PHP file being requested by the attacker. The PHP interpreter forking a shell or recon LOLBin is the classic post-webshell-execution shape and is extremely uncommon in production PHP stacks outside of imagemagick/ffmpeg wrappers, which can be excluded via cmdline. Parent-child pair is the high-fidelity signal — neither side alone qualifies.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.001 T1059.003 T1059.004 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • PHP applications using exec/system to call ImageMagick (convert), ffmpeg, or wkhtmltopdf — flag and allowlist by cmdline
  • WordPress / Drupal cron jobs shelling out to wp-cli or drush from php-fpm
  • Application-installed monitoring agents using whoami/hostname from PHP for diagnostics
  • Composer post-install / post-update scripts running during deploys
  • PHP-based queue workers (php-resque, Laravel Horizon) that legitimately spawn child processes for job isolation
Suppression filter
and not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("convert","ffmpeg","wkhtmltopdf","gs ","ghostscript","imagemagick","wp-cli","drush","artisan","composer")) and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("composer install","composer update","post-install","post-update"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full ProcessCommandLine and InitiatingProcessCommandLine — webshells frequently pass attacker input as the arg (e.g. 'cmd.exe /c whoami'). Pull the upstream PHP request from W3CIISLog/access logs around Timestamp ±5s using ProcessId correlation. 2) Contain: kill the PHP-FPM worker pool (systemctl restart php-fpm or iisreset), block source IP, and pull the on-disk PHP files written by that worker UID in the last 24h for analysis. 3) Hunt: enumerate further child processes from any php-fpm/w3wp in the org over the last 7d (DeviceProcessEvents | parent in PHP set), check for outbound C2 from those workers (DeviceNetworkEvents), and run UC1 to find the webshell artefact.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-fpm.exe","php-cgi.exe","httpd.exe","nginx.exe","w3wp.exe","caddy.exe","php.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh.exe","bash.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","reg.exe","hostname.exe","ipconfig.exe","systeminfo.exe","tasklist.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\curl.exe","\\wget.exe","\\whoami.exe","\\net.exe","\\net1.exe","\\reg.exe","\\hostname.exe","\\ipconfig.exe","\\systeminfo.exe","\\tasklist.exe")

HTTP multipart upload: image Content-Type with PHP/executable filename extension (CVE-2026-48062 exploit shape) AIDelivery High
Detects the exact bypass condition described in the advisory at the request layer: a multipart upload where the Content-Type header indicates an image (image/gif, image/png, image/jpeg) but the multipart filename ends in .php / .phtml / .phar / .phps. CodeIgniter4's pre-4.7.3 ext_in rule trusts the MIME-guessed extension and accepts the file. Requires WAF or application-level HTTP body parsing — IIS / Apache access logs alone do not expose multipart filenames. Rationale: Article names the exact rule: `ext_in[avatar,gif]` is bypassed by `shell.php` containing GIF-like content. The detectable signature at ingress is the multipart-part mismatch: declared Content-Type=image/* AND filename=*.php. WAF / app-tier HTTP logging is required (IIS/Apache plain access logs don't expose multipart filenames), so falcon_logscale_query and defender_kql are intentionally empty — FDR and Defender DeviceNetworkEvents don't carry decoded multipart part headers.
ATT&CKT1190 T1036.008
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal pentest / red-team running automated file-upload bypass tests against the same endpoint
  • Bug-bounty researcher submitting test payloads via a known WAF-allowed source IP
  • Misconfigured client uploading a .php file that the client incorrectly tagged as image/jpeg (rare, usually a browser-side bug)
  • WAF replay/debug traffic from QA environment that has been mirrored into the prod log stream
Suppression filter
and not (SourceIP in ("<pentest-egress-ip>","<bug-bounty-egress-ip>")) and not (UA has_any ("Burp","sqlmap","OWASP ZAP") and SourceIP startswith "10.")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full multipart body from the WAF and confirm whether the file was accepted by the upload endpoint (HTTP 200/302 vs 4xx). Identify the target CodeIgniter4 host(s) and the resolved file path on disk by tracing the SrcIpAddr to backend logs. 2) Contain: block SourceIP at the WAF, drop any uploaded artefact from disk after preserving a forensic copy, and verify CodeIgniter4 framework version >= 4.7.3 on the receiving app. 3) Hunt: search the prior 30d of WAF logs for the same SrcIpAddr against any upload endpoint org-wide, and pivot to UC1 / UC2 to see whether the dropped file was executed.
let UploadEndpoints = dynamic(["/upload","/avatar","/uploads","/file","/profile","/image","/photo","/picture"]);
let ImageMimes = dynamic(["image/gif","image/jpeg","image/jpg","image/png","image/webp","image/bmp","gif","jpeg","png","jpg","webp","bmp"]);

    | where FileType in~ (ImageMimes)

    | project TimeGenerated, Vendor=DeviceVendor, SourceIP, DestHost=DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, FileName, FileType, UA=RequestClientApplication
),
(
    ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
    | where Url has_any (UploadEndpoints)
    | where FileMimeType in~ (ImageMimes)

)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable CodeIgniter4 framework inventory (CVE-2026-48062, < 4.7.3) AIReconnaissance High
Asset-state hunt: enumerates hosts where Defender TVM or Sentinel inventory reports composer:codeigniter4/framework at a version < 4.7.3, scoped by the CVE-2026-48062 advisory. Use this to drive patch deployment and prioritise application-layer monitoring for the run-time detections in UC1-UC3. Rationale: Pure inventory pivot using the CVE explicitly named in the advisory (CVE-2026-48062) and the affected package `composer:codeigniter4/framework` < 4.7.2. Sigma omitted because asset-state inventory is not a single-event-shape detection. Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch omitted because composer-level framework inventory is not in their standard schemas — Defender TVM and Sentinel TVM are the canonical surfaces.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts with CodeIgniter4 vendored under a non-production path (CI runner image, archived backup) which is not actively served
  • Container hosts whose TVM scan reports the package inside a stopped image layer rather than a running container
  • Dev-only laptops with cloned codeigniter4/CodeIgniter4 git source for contributor work
  • Vendored CodeIgniter4 inside a parent application that ships its own patched fork (rare — verify with the app team)
Response runbook
1) Triage: cross-reference each DeviceName with the CMDB to identify owning team, application name, and exposure (internet-facing vs internal). Prioritise IsInternetFacing=true. 2) Contain: open a change ticket to upgrade composer:codeigniter4/framework to >= 4.7.3, and for any host that cannot patch within 72h apply the advisory's listed workarounds (move uploads outside webroot, use $file->store() or $file->move($path, $file->getRandomName()), disable PHP execution in upload dirs). 3) Hunt: enable UC1/UC2/UC3 alerting on the affected hosts and review the prior 30d of WAF logs against any upload endpoints those apps expose.

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)

| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2024-55591", "CVE-2025-32433", "CVE-2025-33073", "CVE-2026-11645", "CVE-2026-20230", "CVE-2026-23479")

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2024-55591", "CVE-2025-32433", "CVE-2025-33073", "CVE-2026-11645", "CVE-2026-20230", "CVE-2026-23479")

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

| sort - click_time

ATT&CKT1027 T1195.002

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Miasma Phantom Gyp: ~157-byte binding.gyp file dropped in package root (npm install code-exec primitive) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Miasma and Hades Are Spreading Now: Detect Them on Developer Machines with Suspi
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Miasma/Hades: AI-agent or editor config file written outside the IDE (auto-exec on project open) · [LLM] Hades PyPI worm: Python interpreter spawns Bun runtime or downloads it from bun.sh/oven-sh · [LLM] Known Miasma/Hades payload SHA256 observed in file write or process execution · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Worm propagation signal: rapid serial npm publish or twine upload from a single developer host
Miasma/Hades: AI-agent or editor config file written outside the IDE (auto-exec on project open) AIInstallation High
Hunts the seven exact dotfile/dotfolder paths the StepSecurity write-up lists as Miasma/Hades auto-execute footholds (.vscode/tasks.json, .vscode/setup.mjs, .claude/setup.mjs, .claude/settings.json, .cursor/rules/setup.mdc, .gemini/settings.json, .github/setup.js). These files trigger code execution when the developer simply opens the folder in VS Code, Cursor, Claude Code or Gemini — no install, no lifecycle script. Suppresses writes initiated by the legitimate IDE binaries themselves so the surfaced events are dropper-style writes (git checkout, archive extraction, package post-install scripts, unsigned utilities). Rationale: Targets the exact seven auto-execute paths in Table 1 of the article. Cross-checked with Snyk and Semgrep write-ups (linked) confirming the Phantom Gyp/IDE-hook delivery primitives. Suppressing the IDE binaries themselves is the key FP cut — only the worm-style drop (npm/git/zip/python writing into another project's dotfolder) survives. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/node-gyp-supply-chain-compromise-self-propagating-npm-worm-binding-gyp/ • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/miasma-v2-self-spreading-npm-worm-now-uses-malicious-bindinggyp-file-and-compromises-57-packages/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/ironworm-and-new-miasma-worm-variant.html
ATT&CKT1546 T1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer cloning a legitimate repo template that already ships .vscode/tasks.json or .github/setup.js
  • yo / cookiecutter / create-react-app scaffolding tools writing IDE config on project bootstrap
  • Personal dotfiles bootstrapper (e.g. chezmoi, stow) seeding ~/.claude/settings.json
  • Anthropic Claude Code installer writing .claude/settings.json into the user profile path
  • Renovate/Dependabot bot committing a CI workflow file under .github/
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("git.exe","npm.exe","node.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("clone","checkout","create-react-app","cookiecutter","yo ")) | where not (FolderPath startswith @"C:\Users\" and FolderPath endswith @"\.claude" and FileName =~ "settings.json" and InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "claude.exe")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — pull the file contents (Defender Live Response `getfile` or LogScale FileWritten WrittenBytes) and inspect: legitimate IDE configs are small, formatted JSON; Miasma/Hades drops carry obfuscated JS, fetch('https://bun.sh/...') strings, base64 blobs, or runOn:folderOpen with a shell payload. Check repo provenance — `git log -- <path>` will show the commit that introduced it. 2) CONTAIN — if malicious: isolate the host via Defender, revoke any cached npm/PyPI/GitHub/AWS tokens belonging to the user (the worm exfils to attacker GitHub repos), and quarantine the project tree. 3) HUNT — pivot on the same SHA256 across the fleet, check that user's recent `npm publish` / `twine upload` activity (UC5), and search GitHub audit logs for new SSH keys or repo creates from that account in the last 72h.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where (FolderPath has @"\.vscode" and FileName in~ ("tasks.json","setup.mjs"))
   or (FolderPath has @"\.claude" and FileName in~ ("setup.mjs","settings.json"))
   or (FolderPath has @"\.cursor\rules" and FileName =~ "setup.mdc")
   or (FolderPath has @"\.gemini" and FileName =~ "settings.json")
   or (FolderPath has @"\.github" and FileName =~ "setup.js")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Code.exe","Code - Insiders.exe","cursor.exe","claude.exe","gemini.exe","windsurf.exe","devenv.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where (TargetFilePath has @"\.vscode" and TargetFileName in~ ("tasks.json","setup.mjs"))
   or (TargetFilePath has @"\.claude" and TargetFileName in~ ("setup.mjs","settings.json"))
   or (TargetFilePath has @"\.cursor\rules" and TargetFileName =~ "setup.mdc")
   or (TargetFilePath has @"\.gemini" and TargetFileName =~ "settings.json")
   or (TargetFilePath has @"\.github" and TargetFileName =~ "setup.js")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("Code.exe","Code - Insiders.exe","cursor.exe","claude.exe","gemini.exe","windsurf.exe","devenv.exe")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSize, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Miasma/Hades AI-Agent or Editor Auto-Execute Config Dropped Outside IDE
id: 6f7f51bb-1d62-4bb5-8c92-4f4e3d2c1aa1
description: Detects creation of the AI-agent / editor configuration files that auto-execute on project open (.vscode/tasks.json runOn:folderOpen, .vscode/setup.mjs, .claude/setup.mjs SessionStart hook, .claude/settings.json, .cursor/rules/setup.mdc, .gemini/settings.json, .github/setup.js) by non-IDE processes — the Miasma/Hades worm foothold technique.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/miasma-and-hades-are-spreading-now-detect-them-on-developer-machines-with-suspicious-files
  - https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/miasma-v2-self-spreading-npm-worm-now-uses-malicious-bindinggyp-file-and-compromises-57-packages/
  - https://snyk.io/blog/node-gyp-supply-chain-compromise-self-propagating-npm-worm-binding-gyp/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/12
tags:
  - attack.t1546
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1059.007
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_vscode_tasks:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\.vscode\tasks.json'
      - '\.vscode\setup.mjs'
  selection_claude:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\.claude\setup.mjs'
      - '\.claude\settings.json'
  selection_cursor:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\.cursor\rules\setup.mdc'
  selection_gemini:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\.gemini\settings.json'
  selection_github:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\.github\setup.js'
  filter_legitimate_ide:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\Code.exe'
      - '\Code - Insiders.exe'
      - '\cursor.exe'
      - '\claude.exe'
      - '\gemini.exe'
      - '\windsurf.exe'
      - '\devenv.exe'
  condition: (1 of selection_*) and not filter_legitimate_ide
falsepositives:
  - Developer copying a project template that already contains these files

Hades PyPI worm: Python interpreter spawns Bun runtime or downloads it from bun.sh/oven-sh AIInstallation High
Detects the Hades PyPI payload: an __init__.py / .pth hook fires on import, downloads a standalone Bun runtime, and executes a JavaScript credential stealer. Python interpreter as the parent of bun.exe (or as the parent of curl/wget/PowerShell fetching bun.sh, bun.com, or github.com/oven-sh/bun release tarballs) is a near-zero-baseline behaviour on normal developer machines. Rationale: Web search corroborated Hades downloads a standalone Bun runtime to run the JS stealer (Phoenix Security, Socket, Semgrep). Python.exe as parent of bun.exe is functionally zero-baseline on dev machines — Bun is a JS runtime, no reason for Python to launch it outside of this attack chain. Hash-blind, so survives the worm mutating its payload. Cross-checked against: • https://phoenix.security/miasma-azure-hades-pypi-supply-chain-worm-2026/ • https://socprime.com/active-threats/miasma-supply-chain-attack-spreads-through-the-phantom-gyp-worm/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/ironworm-and-new-miasma-worm-variant.html
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1105 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Polyglot developer running a Python helper that intentionally bootstraps a Bun-based JS test suite
  • CI agent (GitHub Actions self-hosted runner) on a dev workstation that uses a Python setup-step to install Bun
  • DevOps tooling like uv/poetry plugin invoking Bun via os.system for npm-mirror parity testing
  • Education / tutorial scripts that demonstrate cross-runtime tooling
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.py","conftest.py","poetry","uv ","tox") and ProcessCommandLine has "bun.sh/install" and AccountName !endswith "$" and InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","bash.exe"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — capture the Python parent's full command line and the Python virtualenv path; identify the imported package via `pip show` / `__init__.py` on disk and look for the obfuscated one-liner the article describes. Capture Bun binary SHA256 and any subsequent network egress from bun.exe. 2) CONTAIN — kill the bun.exe and Python process trees, isolate the host, revoke npm/GitHub/AWS/GCP/Azure/Vault/Kubernetes tokens (the documented exfil targets), and yank any cached PyPI token from ~/.pypirc / keyring. 3) HUNT — pivot on the offending PyPI package name across the fleet (`pip list`), check the StepSecurity Hades package list and ensmallen-family packages, and search Bun network egress for attacker-controlled GitHub repos used for token exfiltration.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python3.exe","python3.11.exe","python3.12.exe","python3.13.exe")
| where FileName =~ "bun.exe"
   or (FileName in~ ("curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bitsadmin.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("bun.sh","bun.com/install","oven-sh/bun","bun-windows-","bun-linux-","bun-darwin-"))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentImage=InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildImage=FolderPath, ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python3.exe","python3.11.exe","python3.12.exe","python3.13.exe")
| where TargetProcessName =~ "bun.exe"
   or (TargetProcessName in~ ("curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bitsadmin.exe") and TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("bun.sh","bun.com/install","oven-sh/bun","bun-windows-","bun-linux-","bun-darwin-"))
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Hades PyPI Worm - Python Interpreter Spawns Bun Runtime or Downloads It
id: 8a4d2e0f-3b91-4c25-9a17-71d6c4f08b22
description: Detects the Hades PyPI payload chain — Python imports the malicious package, the __init__.py / .pth startup hook downloads a standalone Bun runtime from bun.sh / github.com/oven-sh/bun, then runs the JavaScript credential stealer. Python spawning bun.exe (or python spawning curl/powershell/wget fetching bun.* artefacts) is the high-confidence pivot.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/miasma-and-hades-are-spreading-now-detect-them-on-developer-machines-with-suspicious-files
  - https://phoenix.security/miasma-azure-hades-pypi-supply-chain-worm-2026/

      - '\python.exe'
      - '\pythonw.exe'
      - '\python3.exe'
      - '\python3.11.exe'
      - '\python3.12.exe'
      - '\python3.13.exe'
  child_bun_direct:

  child_bun_download:

      - 'bun-linux-'
      - 'bun-darwin-'

falsepositives:
  - Developer deliberately installing Bun via a Python helper script (rare; verify)
level: critical
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\python.exe OR *\\pythonw.exe OR *\\python3.exe OR *\\python3.11.exe OR *\\python3.12.exe OR *\\python3.13.exe OR *\\Python.exe) (@Image:(*\\bun.exe OR *\\Bun.exe) OR (@Image:(*\\curl.exe OR *\\wget.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\bitsadmin.exe) AND @CommandLine:(*bun.sh* OR *bun.com/install* OR *oven-sh/bun* OR *bun-windows-* OR *bun-linux-* OR *bun-darwin-*)))

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

Miasma Phantom Gyp: ~157-byte binding.gyp file dropped in package root (npm install code-exec primitive) AIExploitation High
Hunts the Phantom Gyp execution primitive: Miasma ships a 157-byte binding.gyp file that triggers code execution during the native-build phase of npm install, bypassing preinstall/postinstall script scanners entirely. Legitimate binding.gyp files for native node modules are several KB; a tiny binding.gyp landing inside a project tree (and especially being modified by git/npm/archive extraction rather than a developer editor) is the worm's tell. Rationale: The article specifies the binding.gyp is 157 bytes (size predicate <400 gives slack for variant builds). Cross-checked with StepSecurity v1 binding.gyp write-up, Snyk node-gyp supply-chain post, Semgrep Miasma v2 analysis — all converge on the same primitive. Excluding node-gyp's own bundled scaffold is the cleanest baseline cut. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://snyk.io/blog/node-gyp-supply-chain-compromise-self-propagating-npm-worm-binding-gyp/ • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/miasma-v2-self-spreading-npm-worm-now-uses-malicious-bindinggyp-file-and-compromises-57-packages/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007 T1027.013
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • node-addon developer hand-writing a minimal binding.gyp during initial project setup
  • Generator tools like node-addon-api or cmake-js scaffolding a small starter binding.gyp
  • Test fixtures in node-gyp's own test suite (filtered by the node_modules path exclusion)
  • Educational tutorials reproducing 'hello world' native module examples
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "Code.exe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-addon","cmake-js","node-gyp configure")) | where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("git.exe","7z.exe","tar.exe") and FolderPath has @"\node_modules\")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — pull the binding.gyp contents (Live Response getfile or LogScale FileWritten payload). A legitimate stub references `'targets': [{'target_name': '<name>', 'sources': ['*.cc']}]`; Miasma's variant invokes Python actions / shell commands or pulls a remote payload at build time. Cross-check the SHA256 against the article's five hashes. 2) CONTAIN — if malicious, isolate the host, kill any in-flight node-gyp/python.exe descendants, revoke the user's npm publishing token (npm token revoke), and prevent the package from being pushed onward. 3) HUNT — pivot on the package directory name across the fleet, check npm registry audit logs for new versions published from the user's account, and search the StepSecurity Miasma compromised-package list to identify the entry point.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileName =~ "binding.gyp"
| where FileSize < 400
| where FolderPath !has @"\node_modules\node-gyp\"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName =~ "binding.gyp"
| where TargetFileSize < 400
| where TargetFilePath !has @"\node_modules\node-gyp\"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSize, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Known Miasma/Hades payload SHA256 observed in file write or process execution AIInstallation Medium
Direct IOC hit on the five SHA256 hashes the StepSecurity research team published for the Miasma and Hades campaigns. Matches across file writes (worm payload dropped to disk) and process execution (payload run). Hash-based detections are short-lived against a mutating worm but offer high-fidelity catches while the IOCs are still fresh. Rationale: Hashes are from the pre-extracted IOC list in the article. StepSecurity is the originating research source (acknowledged in JFrog and Semgrep follow-ups) so we ship as hunting-grade IOCs; rate them critical because hash collisions are nil and the worm is actively spreading at publish time. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-miasma-redhat-cloud-services/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal malware-analysis sandbox detonating a known sample
  • Threat-intel team copying the sample to a quarantine share for IR
  • Researcher running the sample against an EDR in a lab tenant
  • Backup software replicating quarantined files between tiers
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !startswith "sandbox-" | where DeviceName !startswith "malware-lab-" | where AccountName !in~ ("ir-analyst","threat-intel-svc")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — confirm the hit is on a production developer workstation, not a sandbox / lab host (check DeviceInfo tags). Pull the full process tree and file lineage; note which npm or PyPI package surfaced the payload. 2) CONTAIN — isolate the host immediately, revoke every credential cached on the box (npm, PyPI, GitHub, AWS, GCP, Azure, Vault, Kubernetes — per the documented worm targets), invalidate any in-flight package publish from the user's accounts, and ban the SHA256 fleet-wide via Defender custom indicators. 3) HUNT — search the last 30 days for other devices that touched the same package versions or downloaded artefacts from the same npm/PyPI registry path; pivot on the username for parallel publishing-token theft.
let MiasmaHashes = dynamic([

    "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966"
]);
union
  (DeviceFileEvents

   | project Timestamp, Source="FileEvent", DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Path=FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, ParentImage=InitiatingProcessFileName, Cmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine),

| order by Timestamp desc
